AREA The peak is constructed in such a way, that the area of the delta function is finite, and equal to 1: ∫ ∞ −∞ δ(x)dx = 1

# Page 18^page=18
SIFTING PROPERTY An important property of the Dirac delta function is the sifting property: So the integral of a function multiplied by the delta function is just the function itself at where the delta function peaks. ∫ ∞ −∞ f(x)δ(x − x0)dx = f(x0)

# Page 27^page=27
STOCHASTIC PROCESSES The diffusion equation is similar to Brownian motion. Heat diffusion: particles bounce against each other thereby transferring kinetic energy and hence heat. Order of particles per gram: the diffusion equation is an average description and suffices for heat diffusion. Alternative: model a single particle. The particle will be kicked around by other particles: Brownian motion. Similar to second year module: financial mathematics and econo-physics. It would be good to revise Simon's lecture notes. 1023

EXTENSIONS One can extend this description to geometric Brownian motion ( ), used for (non-negative) stock prices. See also lecture notes of Simon Smith 'Financial mathematics and econo-physics'. A random walk-approach is also used in Diffusion Monte Carlo ( ). This is a technique for solving the Schrodinger equation of many electrons in quantum mechanics. ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK PROCESS Another extension is the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process: where is a Wiener process and is a positive constant. Notice that we now have an extra term as compared to the Wiener process. It forces the value of to not deviate too much from zero. If, for example, is large and positive, then the increment will be more likely to be negative. Note: one may be tempted to write the stochastic differential equation as but the problem is that the Wiener process is not differentiable in time; it is continuous, but the derivative is not continuous. Hence, strictly speaking, one cannot construct an equation involving derivatives of . dV (t) = dW (t) − kV (t)dt (*) W (t) k −kV (t)dt V (t) V (t) dV (t) (*) = −kV (t) + dV (t) dt dW (t) dt W (t) W (t)

LANGEVIN EQUATION An alternative description of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is by using a Langevin equation where is a delta-correlated fluctuating term, . Typically stands for the velocity of a particle. The Langevin equation has benefits and drawbacks: Benefit: it is more closely related to Newton's law. Drawback: one has to be careful for the limit , since derivatives are used. For finite integration steps it can be solved using where is again a normally distributed random variable with unit variance.
